title: A reading plan
hookLine: a little each day or week: Ezra read the law to the people from morning to midday, then day by day through the feast
tomorrow: what did Thoreau read each morning beside a frozen pond?

lines: THE STREET BY THE WATER GATE.
cards: A book bought with real hope can sit on the nightstand for a year, a receipt still marking page twelve. Another gets swallowed in one weekend and forgotten by Tuesday.
The book of Nehemiah has a reading that went another way. The people of Jerusalem gathered in the street before the water gate and asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the book of the law.
He read it aloud "from the morning until midday." And then he didn't stop there.

teach.b: First, the way they read: "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." Not just loud. Clear, with helpers explaining what it meant.

teach.h: GO, EAT, THIS DAY IS HOLY.
teach.b: The people wept as they heard it, and their leaders told them: go, eat and drink and send portions to those who have nothing, for this day is holy.

teach.h: DAY BY DAY, FIRST TO LAST.
teach.b: Then the line that answers the question: "Also day by day, from the first day unto the last day, he read in the book of the law of God." Day by day, through the whole feast. Not one heroic sitting.
A portion each day, explained, then lived. That rhythm runs through Jewish practice.
In synagogues, the Torah is read aloud in public, a portion at a time; the book of Acts mentions Moses being read in the synagogues every Sabbath day.
A little, regularly, together, with someone to give the sense. A reading plan on your own path can borrow all three: a set portion, a set time, and someone to ask what it means.

how: In synagogues the Torah is read aloud in public a portion at a time. People on many paths keep a reading plan: a set passage at a set time each day or week, sometimes with a group or a guide to talk it through.

games.q: a friend's book club picked a thick book and everyone quit by chapter three. by Nehemiah 8, what would help?
o: a short portion each week, read aloud, with time to talk about what it means.
one long weekend marathon to get through the whole thing at once.
everyone reads alone and skips the meeting; discussion slows things down.
games.why: Ezra read day by day, with helpers giving the sense. A little, regularly, together.

practice: Open something you're reading, or recall a line you know well. Read one short passage aloud, slowly and distinctly, then say in your own words what it means. Sit quietly with that sense for the rest of the sit.
